questions.question: What does the per-shard .partial.json state let StreamingDownloader verify before resuming?
options: That the remote server supports every compression format before opening the cache.
That the on-disk partial has exactly verified_bytes and the recorded SHA-256 prefix before it sends a Range request.
That all other shards have completed, so a failed shard can be skipped.
That the JSONL tokenizer has already consumed the shard and can discard the compressed bytes.
questions.explanation: _verify_partial compares the file size with verified_bytes and recomputes the prefix hash. A mismatch causes the partial and checkpoint to be discarded rather than appended blindly.

questions.question: What does the LSH band scheme buy that exact-hash dedup does not?
options: Constant memory usage
Lossless compression
Sub-linear lookup that flags near-duplicates with high Jaccard similarity even when the documents differ by a few tokens
Faster sha256 computation
questions.explanation: MinHash plus LSH catches paraphrases and boilerplate variants that exact-hash dedup walks past.

questions.question: The downloader writes the next checkpoint before out.write(buf). What happens if the process dies between those two calls?
options: The file is longer than the checkpoint, so the downloader silently appends the same bytes a second time.
The rolling hash is lost, but the file is accepted because the byte count is authoritative.
The checkpoint is written only after the complete shard, so a mid-shard crash cannot affect resume.
The checkpoint can claim bytes that are not yet on disk; the next _verify_partial sees the size mismatch and restarts instead of resuming the invalid partial.
questions.explanation: The write-ahead ordering may leave checkpoint metadata ahead of the file, but _verify_partial rejects that state because the file size must equal verified_bytes. The safe fallback is to delete the partial and restart.

questions.question: What does the manifest lock file protect?
options: It stores a digest of the manifest so a consumer can detect content changes before trusting the shard inventory.
It makes every shard download single-threaded and prevents Range requests.
It records only the wall-clock time of the last downloader process.
It replaces the compressed shard files so downstream code never reads them.
questions.explanation: ManifestWriter writes the manifest and a .json.lock containing its SHA-256. Consumers can compare the digest and notice an edited or mismatched manifest.

questions.question: Why is dedup placed upstream of tokenization rather than after?
options: The tokenizer cannot read JSONL
Tokenization is expensive; running it twice on the same document doubles cost for no loss-curve benefit, so dropping duplicates first is strictly cheaper
Tokenizers reject duplicates
The tokenizer needs a vocabulary first
questions.explanation: Dedup is the first stage where each duplicate-dropped document saves the tokenizer one pass.

questions.question: What does tombstoning a dropped duplicate preserve that a silent delete does not?
options: Disk space
Compression ratio
The link between the duplicate and the keeper it collided with, plus an audit trail that survives a later threshold change
Manifest sha256 stability
questions.explanation: Tombstones let a future pass revisit the dedup threshold; deletes lose the evidence.
